VIDEO.title: Jesus Revealed His Secret And It Broke Him
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Matthew 19:13-30 · Episode 38 (#41 of 58 in the playlist)
hand: With people this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 19:13-30. Children are brought to Jesus for Him to lay hands on them and pray; the disciples rebuke them, but Jesus says the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these. A young man asks what good thing he must do to have eternal life. Jesus lists commandments; the man says he has kept them all; Jesus tells him to sell his possessions, give to the poor and follow Him, and he goes away grieving. It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom. With God all things are possible. The Twelve will sit on twelve thrones in the regeneration.

Like a good rabbi, Jesus uses what happens around Him to teach. Children were negligible in society, yet He welcomes them, living out 'the last, first.' Luke tells us the man was a ruler; he seems to ask a genuine question, but a flawed one.

Jesus' reply, 'There is only One who is good,' echoes the refrain 'He indeed is good for His lovingkindness endures forever' (2 Chronicles 5:13). The right question is not what accomplishment earns eternal life but how to know God. Flawless obedience was never possible (Deuteronomy 27:26; Galatians 3:10).

'If you wish to be complete' uses the word of Matthew 5:48, the Hebrew idea of tamim: whole, mature, loving without partiality. Giving to the poor is lending to Yahweh (Proverbs 19:17). The disciples are astonished because wealth was seen as a sign of God's approval.

The lesson: no one can earn their way into God's kingdom. What is required to enter it is the same thing needed to thrive as a child of God: forsaking all daily to know God, holding everything with open hands.
QUOTES: No one can earn their way into God's kingdom.
The world's mammon can very easily distract us from relying on God's manna.
Forsaking all daily to know God.
We never outgrow the gospel. We simply grow more and more into the gospel.

method.p: The rich man arrives right after Jesus welcomes the children, and right after chapter 18's 'become like children.' The teacher asks why: it is not random. Read neighboring scenes together and one becomes the living illustration of the other.

LSB_QUOTES.text: Jesus said to him, “If you wish to be complete, go and sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me.”
And looking at them Jesus said to them, “With people this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”
And this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent.

src.text: Then some children were brought to Him so that He might lay His hands on them and pray; and the disciples rebuked them. But Jesus said, “Let the children alone, and do not hinder them from coming to Me; for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.”

lines.text: Like a good rabbi, Jesus uses situations around Him to teach. He welcomes children to teach again the importance of humility, one chapter after 18:1-4.
The video cites D. A. Carson that children were negligible members of first-century society. No one is better than or too important for these little outcasts.

src.text: But many who are first will be last; and the last, first.

lines.text: Jesus ends the chapter with these words. In welcoming the children He is living this principle out for the disciples to witness.

left.text: and said, “Truly I say to you, unless you are converted and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.

right.text: And behold, someone came to Him and said, “Teacher, what good thing shall I do that I may have eternal life?”

lines.text: Jesus has just taught that they must humble themselves like a child. Then this rich person shows up: a living, breathing illustration of the antithesis, so the lesson sinks down deep.

left.text: The young man *said to Him, “All these things I have kept; what am I still lacking?”

right.text: And a ruler questioned Him, saying, “Good Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?”

lines.text: Matthew tells us he is young (19:20); Luke that he is a ruler. The video mentions Craig Blomberg's suggestion that he was a synagogue official.
Unlike the Pharisees, he does not seem to be laying a trap. His question is genuine, but fundamentally flawed.

left.text: And He said to him, “Why are you asking Me about what is good? There is only One who is good; but if you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.”

right.text: in unison when the trumpeters and the singers were to make themselves heard with one voice to praise and to give thanks to Yahweh, and when they lifted up their voice accompanied by trumpets and cymbals and instruments of music, and when they praised Yahweh saying, “He indeed is good for His lovingkindness endures forever,” then the house, the house of Yahweh, was filled with a cloud,

lines.text: Jesus' answer comes out of a refrain repeated in Psalm 106:1, Psalm 118:1, 1 Chronicles 16 and 2 Chronicles 5: the Lord is good, and His lovingkindness endures forever.
The right question is not 'What accomplishment earns eternal life?' but 'How can I know God?' Jesus is already answering, in a veiled, very Jewish way.

RULER.title: Cursed is he who does not confirm

left.text: ‘Cursed is he who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them.’ And all the people shall say, ‘Amen.’

right.text: For as many as are of the works of the Law are under a curse, for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who does not abide by all things written in the book of the law, to do them.”

lines.text: Flawless obedience was never a real possibility. Obedience begins in recognizing who God is, the only One who is good, and who we are before Him.
Perhaps that is why we are told he is young: brash enough to suggest anyone could keep the totality of the law.

RULER.title: If you wish to be complete

left.text: Jesus said to him, “If you wish to be complete, go and sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me.”

right.text: Therefore you are to be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.

lines.text: Jesus lists commandments and adds 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' (Leviticus 19:18). Then He rephrases that command with a specific example the man cannot do, revealing he has not kept it.
It is the same Greek word as 5:48, where 'perfect' means loving with no partiality. The idea is the Hebrew tamim: complete, morally mature, even innocent; not flawless as we use it today.

src.text: He who is gracious to a poor man lends to Yahweh, / And He will repay him for his bountiful deed.

lines.text: When he says he has kept even 'love your neighbor,' Jesus takes him to this proverb on wealth and charity. Give to the poor and you lend to God, who repays with heavenly treasure.
Wealth is a temporary blessing to be shared. Maybe he knew exactly what Jesus meant, saw his shortcomings, and still went away grieving (19:22).

KINGDOM.title: A camel through the eye of a needle

src.text: And again I say to you, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.”

lines.text: The man asked about eternal life; Jesus answers with 'the kingdom of heaven' (19:23) and 'the kingdom of God' (19:24). He treats them as synonymous.
The camel was the largest animal in the land and the needle's eye the smallest opening: an impossible picture.

src.text: And when the disciples heard this, they were very astonished and said, “Then who can be saved?” And looking at them Jesus said to them, “With people this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”

lines.text: The disciples probably held the view that material wealth was a blessing from God and a sign of His approval. If an obedient man blessed by God can't enter, who can?
It is impossible if you think you can earn your way. Entering must be done with God: a humble reliance on Him that overflows from a relationship with Him.

left.text: And Jesus said to them, “Truly I say to you, that you who have followed Me, in the regeneration when the Son of Man will sit on His glorious throne, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

right.text: And to Him was given dominion, / Glory, and a kingdom, / That all the peoples, nations, and men of every tongue / Might serve Him. / His dominion is an everlasting dominion / Which will not be taken away; / And His kingdom is one / Which will not be destroyed.

lines.text: 'The new world' in the video's translation is the regeneration or renewal, the consummation of the kingdom mentioned in Acts 3, Romans 8 and 2 Peter 3. Jesus looks back to Isaiah 65:17 and Daniel 7.
In a kingdom there are thrones. When the Son of Man has dominion and glory, the Twelve will judge the twelve tribes.

KINGDOM.title: Forsaking all daily to know God

lines.text: No one can earn their way into God's kingdom; for someone with that mindset, blessings can become a distraction. What is required to enter is what is needed to thrive: forsaking all daily to know God, with open hands.
The kingdom is a return to the Eden-like relationship Adam and Eve had with their Creator. That is why Jesus defines eternal life as knowing God (John 17:3).

Many of us slip into a rich-ruler mindset, as if what we do for God gives us status with Him. The video recalls Tim Keller contrasting a business relationship (I work to belong) with a family one (I belong, so I work).

TERMS.def: The life of the age to come; Jesus treats it as entering the kingdom (19:16, 23-24) and defines it as knowing God (John 17:3).
Hebrew: complete, whole, blameless, morally mature (Deuteronomy 18:13).
Greek palingenesia: the renewal of all things; 'the new world' in some translations.
Daniel's title for God enthroned, before whom the Son of Man comes.
Wealth as a rival master (6:24); the video sets it against God's manna.

WORDS.gloss: Eternal, of the age to come.
Regeneration, renewal. Look up: BDAG, παλιγγενεσία.
Complete, whole, blameless. Look up: BDB or HALOT, תמים.

BACKGROUND.p: Deuteronomy ties prosperity to covenant faithfulness (Deuteronomy 28:1-14), and many in Jesus' day read riches as a sign of God's approval. That helps explain the disciples' astonishment.
Parents brought children to rabbis and elders for a blessing with the laying on of hands, as Jacob blessed Ephraim and Manasseh (Genesis 48:14).
A later story that 'the needle's eye' was a small gate in Jerusalem has no ancient evidence. The Talmud uses a similar impossible picture with an elephant (Berakhot 55b).

DEBATES.p: Some read 'sell your possessions' as a call to this man whose wealth ruled him; others as a counsel for some disciples; others as a standing call to hold everything with open hands. The video takes the last view.

DEBATES.h: Why 'Why are you asking Me about what is good?'
DEBATES.p: Matthew's wording differs from Mark and Luke ('Why do you call Me good?'). Interpreters discuss whether Jesus is pointing to His own identity or simply to God as the source of goodness.
Readers differ on whether the twelve tribes means ethnic Israel restored, or the whole people of God, and whether 'judging' means condemning or ruling.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video says Jesus 'engages with children and heals them' in 13-15; the text says He laid His hands on them and prayed, with no healing.
The video calls 19:16 the only mention of eternal life in Matthew; the phrase returns in 19:29 and 25:46.
The video cites the curse verse as Deuteronomy 27:18; the words it quotes are Deuteronomy 27:26 (27:18 is about misleading a blind person).
The video cites Daniel 7:3 for the Son of Man's kingdom; the passage it then reads is Daniel 7:13-14.

The video says Jesus lists the sixth through tenth commandments; He lists murder, adultery, stealing and false witness, then honoring parents (the fifth), and adds Leviticus 19:18. Coveting, the tenth, is not listed.
The views attributed to D. A. Carson and Craig Blomberg, and the Tim Keller remark, are given without a source; the Keller line is a paraphrase.
In 19:22-23 the LSB has 'went away grieving' and 'it is hard,' where the video reads sorrowful and only with difficulty.
The captions write 'Blombberg' and 'Blumbberg' for Blomberg, and 'Proverbsap' for Proverbs.

QUESTIONS: Why might the disciples have turned the children away?
What was flawed about 'What good thing shall I do?'
How does Proverbs 19:17 change the way you see what you own?
What is the 'one thing' that might be holding you back from following Jesus fully?
Do you relate to God more like a business or a family? What shows it?
What would 'forsaking all daily to know God' look like tomorrow morning?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson, stated plainly: no one can earn their way into God's kingdom; for someone with that mindset, blessings become a distraction. What is required to enter the kingdom is what is required to live and thrive in it: forsaking all daily to know God, with open hands, humbly pursuing the Lord wherever He leads. The teacher admits slipping into the rich ruler's mindset, as if doing things for God earns status with Him. A mentor's saying sums it up: it is the gospel that saves and the gospel that sanctifies; we never outgrow the gospel. Everything we do for our heavenly Father must come out of the overflow of our relationship with Him.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): before you start tomorrow's tasks for God, spend a few quiet minutes with Him first. Read John 17:3 and name one thing you are holding tightly; open your hands over it in prayer.

## Summary (from the video)
- The teacher reads Matthew 19:13-30. Children are brought to Jesus for Him to lay hands on them and pray; the disciples rebuke them, but Jesus says the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these. A young man asks what good thing he must do to have eternal life. Jesus lists commandments; the man says he has kept them all; Jesus tells him to sell his possessions, give to the poor and follow Him, and he goes away grieving. It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom. With God all things are possible. The Twelve will sit on twelve thrones in the regeneration.
- Like a good rabbi, Jesus uses what happens around Him to teach. Children were negligible in society, yet He welcomes them, living out 'the last, first.' Luke tells us the man was a ruler; he seems to ask a genuine question, but a flawed one.
- Jesus' reply, 'There is only One who is good,' echoes the refrain 'He indeed is good for His lovingkindness endures forever' (2 Chronicles 5:13). The right question is not what accomplishment earns eternal life but how to know God. Flawless obedience was never possible (Deuteronomy 27:26; Galatians 3:10).
- 'If you wish to be complete' uses the word of Matthew 5:48, the Hebrew idea of tamim: whole, mature, loving without partiality. Giving to the poor is lending to Yahweh (Proverbs 19:17). The disciples are astonished because wealth was seen as a sign of God's approval.
- The lesson: no one can earn their way into God's kingdom. What is required to enter it is the same thing needed to thrive as a child of God: forsaking all daily to know God, holding everything with open hands.

## Key quotes from the video (auto-captions, lightly cleaned)
> "No one can earn their way into God's kingdom."
> "The world's mammon can very easily distract us from relying on God's manna."
> "Forsaking all daily to know God."
> "We never outgrow the gospel. We simply grow more and more into the gospel."

### Notice the scene next door
The rich man arrives right after Jesus welcomes the children, and right after chapter 18's 'become like children.' The teacher asks why: it is not random. Read neighboring scenes together and one becomes the living illustration of the other.

   (video) It is the same Greek word as 5:48, where 'perfect' means loving with no partiality. The idea is the Hebrew tamim: complete, morally mature, even innocent; not flawless as we use it today.
4. Proverbs 19:17: Lending to Yahweh
   Remez Proverbs 19:17: "He who is gracious to a poor man lends to Yahweh, / And He will repay him for his bountiful deed." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Proverbs+19:17
   (video) When he says he has kept even 'love your neighbor,' Jesus takes him to this proverb on wealth and charity. Give to the poor and you lend to God, who repays with heavenly treasure.
   (video) Wealth is a temporary blessing to be shared. Maybe he knew exactly what Jesus meant, saw his shortcomings, and still went away grieving (19:22). (Matthew 19:22)

## Then who can be saved?
1. Matthew 19:23-24: A camel through the eye of a needle
   Hyperbole Matthew 19:24: "And again I say to you, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+19:24
   (video) The man asked about eternal life; Jesus answers with 'the kingdom of heaven' (19:23) and 'the kingdom of God' (19:24). He treats them as synonymous.
   [Background] The camel was the largest animal in the land and the needle's eye the smallest opening: an impossible picture.
2. Matthew 19:25-26: Then who can be saved?
   Astonished Matthew 19:25-26: "And when the disciples heard this, they were very astonished and said, “Then who can be saved?” And looking at them Jesus said to them, “With people this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+19:25-26
   (video) The disciples probably held the view that material wealth was a blessing from God and a sign of His approval. If an obedient man blessed by God can't enter, who can?
   (video) It is impossible if you think you can earn your way. Entering must be done with God: a humble reliance on Him that overflows from a relationship with Him.
3. Matthew 19:28; Daniel 7:13-14: In the regeneration
   Jesus (Matthew 19:28, LSB): "And Jesus said to them, “Truly I say to you, that you who have followed Me, in the regeneration when the Son of Man will sit on His glorious throne, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel."
   Daniel (Daniel 7:14, LSB): "And to Him was given dominion, / Glory, and a kingdom, / That all the peoples, nations, and men of every tongue / Might serve Him. / His dominion is an everlasting dominion / Which will not be taken away; / And His kingdom is one / Which will not be destroyed."
   (video) 'The new world' in the video's translation is the regeneration or renewal, the consummation of the kingdom mentioned in Acts 3, Romans 8 and 2 Peter 3. Jesus looks back to Isaiah 65:17 and Daniel 7. (Acts 3:21; Isaiah 65:17)
   (video) In a kingdom there are thrones. When the Son of Man has dominion and glory, the Twelve will judge the twelve tribes.
4. The lesson; John 17:3: Forsaking all daily to know God
   (video) No one can earn their way into God's kingdom; for someone with that mindset, blessings can become a distraction. What is required to enter is what is needed to thrive: forsaking all daily to know God, with open hands.
   (video) The kingdom is a return to the Eden-like relationship Adam and Eve had with their Creator. That is why Jesus defines eternal life as knowing God (John 17:3). (John 17:3)
   (video) Many of us slip into a rich-ruler mindset, as if what we do for God gives us status with Him. The video recalls Tim Keller contrasting a business relationship (I work to belong) with a family one (I belong, so I work).

## Key people
- The children: Brought for blessing; welcomed as examples of the humility the kingdom needs. [Background] Mark says Jesus took them in His arms (Mark 10:16).
- The rich young ruler: Asks a genuine but flawed question and goes away grieving. [Background] Mark adds, 'looking at him, Jesus loved him' (Mark 10:21).
- Simon Peter: Asks what the disciples will have, who left everything. [Background] He had left his nets at Jesus' call (4:20).
- The Twelve: Promised twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. [Background] Luke places a similar promise at the Last Supper (Luke 22:30).
- Son of Man: Will sit on His glorious throne, as in Daniel 7. [Background] Matthew returns to the throne scene in 25:31.

## Places [Background]
- Perea: 'Judea beyond the Jordan' (19:1); the setting continues.
- Capernaum: Where Peter left home and nets to follow (19:27).
- Jericho: On the road ahead (20:29).
- Jerusalem: Where Jesus is heading (20:17).

## Key terms
- Eternal life: The life of the age to come; Jesus treats it as entering the kingdom (19:16, 23-24) and defines it as knowing God (John 17:3).
- Tamim: Hebrew: complete, whole, blameless, morally mature (Deuteronomy 18:13).
- Regeneration: Greek palingenesia: the renewal of all things; 'the new world' in some translations.
- Ancient of Days: Daniel's title for God enthroned, before whom the Son of Man comes. [Background]
- Mammon: Wealth as a rival master (6:24); the video sets it against God's manna.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Wealth as blessing: Deuteronomy ties prosperity to covenant faithfulness (Deuteronomy 28:1-14), and many in Jesus' day read riches as a sign of God's approval. That helps explain the disciples' astonishment.
- Blessing children: Parents brought children to rabbis and elders for a blessing with the laying on of hands, as Jacob blessed Ephraim and Manasseh (Genesis 48:14).
- The camel and the needle: A later story that 'the needle's eye' was a small gate in Jerusalem has no ancient evidence. The Talmud uses a similar impossible picture with an elephant (Berakhot 55b).

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "And wherefore did the disciples repel the little children? For dignity." Homilies on Matthew 62, on 19:13-15. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "blaming not riches but them that are held in subjection by them." Homilies on Matthew 63, on 19:23. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "It is not then enough to despise wealth, but we must also maintain poor men, and above all things follow Christ" Homilies on Matthew 63, on 19:21. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Is 19:21 for everyone? Some read 'sell your possessions' as a call to this man whose wealth ruled him; others as a counsel for some disciples; others as a standing call to hold everything with open hands. The video takes the last view.
- Why 'Why are you asking Me about what is good?' Matthew's wording differs from Mark and Luke ('Why do you call Me good?'). Interpreters discuss whether Jesus is pointing to His own identity or simply to God as the source of goodness.
- Twelve thrones Readers differ on whether the twelve tribes means ethnic Israel restored, or the whole people of God, and whether 'judging' means condemning or ruling.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video says Jesus 'engages with children and heals them' in 13-15; the text says He laid His hands on them and prayed, with no healing.
- The video calls 19:16 the only mention of eternal life in Matthew; the phrase returns in 19:29 and 25:46.
- The video cites the curse verse as Deuteronomy 27:18; the words it quotes are Deuteronomy 27:26 (27:18 is about misleading a blind person).
- The video cites Daniel 7:3 for the Son of Man's kingdom; the passage it then reads is Daniel 7:13-14.
- The video says Jesus lists the sixth through tenth commandments; He lists murder, adultery, stealing and false witness, then honoring parents (the fifth), and adds Leviticus 19:18. Coveting, the tenth, is not listed.
- The views attributed to D. A. Carson and Craig Blomberg, and the Tim Keller remark, are given without a source; the Keller line is a paraphrase.
- In 19:22-23 the LSB has 'went away grieving' and 'it is hard,' where the video reads sorrowful and only with difficulty.
- The captions write 'Blombberg' and 'Blumbberg' for Blomberg, and 'Proverbsap' for Proverbs.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why might the disciples have turned the children away?
2. What was flawed about 'What good thing shall I do?'
3. How does Proverbs 19:17 change the way you see what you own?
4. What is the 'one thing' that might be holding you back from following Jesus fully?
5. Do you relate to God more like a business or a family? What shows it?
6. What would 'forsaking all daily to know God' look like tomorrow morning?

## Application
- (video) The lesson, stated plainly: no one can earn their way into God's kingdom; for someone with that mindset, blessings become a distraction. What is required to enter the kingdom is what is required to live and thrive in it: forsaking all daily to know God, with open hands, humbly pursuing the Lord wherever He leads. The teacher admits slipping into the rich ruler's mindset, as if doing things for God earns status with Him. A mentor's saying sums it up: it is the gospel that saves and the gospel that sanctifies; we never outgrow the gospel. Everything we do for our heavenly Father must come out of the overflow of our relationship with Him.
- Study note (added): before you start tomorrow's tasks for God, spend a few quiet minutes with Him first. Read John 17:3 and name one thing you are holding tightly; open your hands over it in prayer.
